instructions: What is a person who types `search_term` into the App Store search box looking for?
Someone typed `search_term` into the App Store search box. Decide what they are trying to find. Use `top_results` only as hints.

instructions.task: Classify the App Store search query `search_term` by what the searcher wants.
instructions.hint: Names of clinics, companies, publishers or specific apps mean they want that one entity; plain topic words mean a need that any good app could serve.

instructions: Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. If the words identify one particular company, publisher, app, clinic or practice (even when built from ordinary words, or ending in LLC, PC, Inc or a city), they want that one entity. If the words only describe a topic, task, exam or tool that many apps could serve, they want a need. Use `top_results` only as supporting evidence.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. A query naming one specific practice, clinic, shop or school wants that one organization, even if it is built from ordinary words such as an adjective plus a service plus 'clinic', 'center' or 'studio' (e.g. 'elite physical therapy clinic'). A query that only names a topic, exam or task, with no sign of one particular business, is a need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. A well-known named product, app, company or publisher (even one whose name is made of ordinary words, like 'hinge health', or a game title, like 'subway surfers') is a brand: they want that one entity. Choose game only for a request to play a type of game or simulator ('welding simulator game'), not for the exact title of one particular game. Plain topic words with no sign of one named entity are a need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. Pick jobs only when the words ask for openings, hiring, careers or staffing (e.g. 'welder jobs near me'). A profession word next to a proper name or acronym of an organization or product (e.g. 'nala paralegal', where NALA is an association) is a brand, not jobs. Plain topic words are a need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. Pick jobs for any query about hiring or being hired, from either side: 'hiring electricians near me', 'welder jobs', 'travel nurse staffing'. The words hiring, jobs, careers, openings, staffing or 'near me' next to a profession signal job listings, not a tool. A title that is the exact name of one well-known game (e.g. 'clash royale') is a brand, not game. Plain topic words with none of these signals are a need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. Three traps: (1) the exact title of one well-known game or app (e.g. 'subway surfers', 'clash royale') is a brand, not game; game is only for generic play words ('fireman plumber', 'forklift simulator'). (2) A profession word beside an organization name or acronym (e.g. 'nala paralegal') is a brand, not local_business or jobs. (3) 'hiring', 'jobs', 'careers', 'staffing' or 'openings' next to a profession (e.g. 'hiring electricians near me') is jobs, not need. Plain topic words with none of these signals are a need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. If the query asks for people to hire or places that are hiring (words like 'hiring', 'jobs', 'staffing', 'careers', 'near me' attached to an occupation), they want job listings, even though the occupation itself is a plain topic word; choose need only when they want a tool or reference for the work. A exact title of one particular game or app is brand or game by that title, not a need.

Classify `search_term` by checking in this order and stopping at the first match. 1) Does it contain hiring words (hiring, jobs, careers, staffing, openings) beside an occupation? -> jobs. 2) Is it the name of one specific product, app, game title or publisher (even a very famous mobile game such as 'clash royale')? -> brand. 3) Is it a proper name of one organization, practice or school (often a person or place name plus a profession, an acronym or LLC)? -> local_business, unless it is clearly a product -> brand. 4) Does it ask for a generic game or simulator to play, with no title? -> game. 5) Is it plain words for a topic, exam, task or tool? -> need. Otherwise other.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants, checking in this order. (1) Does it ask for jobs, hiring or staffing, or is it a job title with 'relief', 'locum' or 'near me' (e.g. 'relief vet tech')? => jobs. (2) Is it the name of one specific organization (credit union, florist, spa, clinic, often with PC, LLC, CC or a person's or place name)? => local_business. (3) Does it ask to play something, with words like 'game' or 'games' next to a trade or hobby (e.g. 'florist game', 'sailing games')? => game. (4) Is it the exact title of one well-known app or game? => brand. (5) Otherwise plain topic or tool words (e.g. 'magnifier', 'jet lag') => need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. A famous game title typed alone (e.g. 'subway surfers', 'clash royale') names one specific product, so answer brand, not game; answer game only for a generic request to play something with no title. A job title with 'hiring', 'jobs' or 'near me' wanting people to employ (e.g. 'hiring electricians near me') is jobs, not need. A proper name of one practice, firm or school (e.g. 'nala paralegal') is local_business. Plain topic or tool words are need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. Hiring words ('hiring', 'jobs', 'staffing') beside an occupation mean jobs. The exact title of one popular game or app ('minecraft', 'candy crush saga') is a brand, not a game. Generic play wording ('truck driving simulator') is a game. A business name with LLC, PC, a city or a person's name is local_business. Plain topic, exam or tool words ('cdl practice test') are a need.

Classify `search_term` by what the searcher wants. Two quick checks first: (1) does it name one specific game or app by its exact title (subway surfers, clash royale)? then brand; (2) does it contain 'hiring', 'jobs', 'near me' with an employer-side wording such as 'hiring electricians near me'? then jobs. A named paralegal or firm (nala paralegal) is local_business. Otherwise a topic, tool or exam is a need.

Classify `search_term` typed into the App Store. Decide by what the searcher wants to obtain: a tool/reference/exam-prep for a profession or task (need); one named app, company or publisher, including popular game titles (brand); one local organization (local_business); something to play (game); or job openings/hiring, including phrases like 'hiring X near me' (jobs). Plain nouns or 'X near me' with 'hiring'/'jobs' are jobs, not need.

Classify `search_term` by what the searcher wants. Rules, in order: (1) hiring, jobs, careers, staffing or openings beside an occupation, including 'hiring X near me' => jobs, never need. (2) The exact title of one known game or app (subway surfers, clash royale, minecraft) => brand, not game; game is only for generic play wording such as 'truck driving simulator'. (3) A profession word attached to an association, publisher or product acronym (nala paralegal, nclex pocket prep) => brand; a clinic, shop or practice named by a place or person plus a service (bridgewater dental) => local_business. (4) Plain topic, exam or tool words => need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. Hiring, 'jobs', 'hiring near me' or 'now hiring' wording means jobs, even when a trade (electrician, plumber) is named. A bare title of one game or app ('clash royale', 'duolingo') is a brand, never game; a company or clinic name ('nala paralegal', 'mayo clinic app') is brand or local_business. Only a plain request for a tool, chart or topic ('pipe fitting chart') is need.

Decide what the person typing `search_term` wants. A famous game or app title typed alone (e.g. a name you recognise as a published mobile game) is a brand, not a game: the searcher wants that one title. 'game' is only for generic wishes to play something. Phrases about hiring or work ('near me', 'jobs', 'hiring', 'openings') are jobs even when they name a trade. A name containing a person's name plus a service word is local_business. Use `top_results` only as supporting evidence.

instructions: Is `search_term` a proper name - the brand, product, company or app name of one specific app or company - rather than plain words describing what the searcher needs? Use `top_results` as evidence: a brand usually appears as the distinctive title of one result.

Would a typical person read `search_term` as the name of one particular product, app, company, publisher, clinic or person, rather than a description of a task or topic? Invented words, trademarks, company or person names, and app titles with taglines are names.

instructions.question: Is `search_term` a name (of one app, product, company, publisher, clinic or person) rather than a description of a need?
instructions.evidence: Check `top_results`: if one result's title or developer contains the distinctive words of `search_term`, it is probably that result's name. If many results share the words, they are probably generic.

instructions: Does `search_term` identify one specific named product, app, company, publisher, publication or person? A name can be built from ordinary words (like 'Paramedic Coach', 'Hinge Health', 'Pharmacy Technician Letter'); a description of a topic, exam or tool is not a name. Use `top_results` only as supporting evidence: many results with similar titles means generic words, one distinctive title or publisher means a name.

instructions.question: Does `search_term` read like the exact title or name of ONE app, company or publisher, rather than a phrase a person would type to find any app for a task?
instructions.steps: 1) If the first result's title (or its developer name) equals `search_term` or nearly equals it, answer true. 2) A title with a colon, dash, tagline, 'app' suffix or a trailing word like 'driver', 'coach', 'letter' still counts as a title. 3) If many results repeat the same words in different titles, answer false.

instructions: Imagine the App Store search results for `search_term`. If one result is clearly 'the' app being asked for (its title or publisher repeats the distinctive words of `search_term`, even with a tagline, an 'app' suffix or a word like coach, driver or letter), answer true. If the words are an exam name, a year, 'prep', 'practice test', 'flashcards', a topic or a tool type that many results share, answer false.

Is `search_term` the title of ONE app or the name of one publisher? Compare it with the first 3 titles in `top_results`: if one title is `search_term` plus at most a tagline, a number or a word like 'app', 'coach', 'driver', 'letter' or 'test', answer true even if the words look ordinary. If the words are only a topic, tool type or exam that several unrelated developers use in their titles, answer false.

Decide whether `search_term` is the NAME of one specific app or publisher. Test: remove a trailing tagline, 'app', 'test', 'prep', year or role word (coach, driver, letter) from the first result's title and from `search_term`; if the remaining distinctive words match and the phrase is how that one app is titled, answer true even when the words look generic (e.g. 'personal trainer prep: test'). If instead several different publishers' results all repeat the same words, the phrase is a topic and the answer is false.

Is `search_term` essentially the title of ONE app in `top_results`, or the name of one clinic, company or person behind it? Ignore whether the words look ordinary or descriptive: if the first results' titles or developer names contain all the distinctive words of `search_term` (even a long phrase like 'check in tools for the joint chiropractic clinics' or 'pilot driver app'), answer true. Answer false only when the words are a topic, exam, year or tool type repeated across many unrelated developers' titles.

Count how many of the first 10 `top_results` titles contain the distinctive words of `search_term`. If exactly one or two titles (or one publisher) carry them and the rest of the list is about other things, `search_term` is that app's or publisher's name: answer true, even when the words look ordinary (e.g. 'paramedic coach', 'pilot driver app'). If three or more results from different publishers share the words, or the words are an exam, certification, year, 'review', 'prep' or tool type (e.g. 'paramedic airway review'), answer false.

Look at the first result for `search_term`. If its title (ignoring case, punctuation, a tagline after a colon or dash, or a suffix like 'app', 'pro', 'coach', 'driver', 'letter', 'test') is the same words as `search_term`, or its developer name is, answer true. If `search_term` is only a topic, exam, role, or tool type that several unrelated results also use in their titles (for example 'pharmacy technician exam prep'), answer false.

Answer true only if `search_term` works as a NAME: the first results' titles or developer names repeat its distinctive words as a title (a company, publisher, person, invented word, or an app title with tagline), or the searcher clearly wants that one app. Answer false when the words just describe a subject, exam, skill, review, job or tool (e.g. 'paramedic airway review', 'welding settings', 'pharmacy technician certification exam test prep'), even if one app happens to use the same words as its title; also count one-word or two-word generic subjects as false unless a distinctive word is the app's own coined name.

Answer true only when one of the first results has a title or developer name that contains ALL the distinctive words of `search_term` (ignoring case, punctuation and filler words such as app, pro, the), so the search is plainly aimed at that one app or organization. Answer false when no result carries those words together, or when the words are only a subject plus a generic word like review, guide, prep, notes, exam or tool that several unrelated apps share (e.g. 'paramedic airway review', 'chiropractic exam prep').

Decide in two steps. Step 1: find the result whose title or developer shares the most distinctive words with `search_term` (ignore generic words such as app, pro, prep, exam, review, guide, test, notes, coach, letter, driver). Step 2: answer true only if that result's title/developer is essentially `search_term` itself (an exact or near-exact title, possibly with a tagline) and the distinctive words are not just a profession or topic that many other results also contain; a profession plus a generic word (e.g. 'paramedic airway review') is false unless one publisher or title clearly owns that exact phrase, while an exact app or publisher title (e.g. 'paramedic coach', 'pharmacy technician letter') is true.

Answer true only when `search_term` is a proper name of one particular app, product or publisher that appears (nearly verbatim) in the top results' names or developers. Answer false when it is generic words for a topic, exam, profession or task, even when several results contain those words, and when it is only a profession plus a generic word such as 'prep', 'review', 'guide', 'log' or 'test'. If you can't point to the one result it names, answer false.

Is `search_term` the name of ONE specific app or publisher? Answer true if a result's title is `search_term` itself (even a short, plain-sounding one like 'Paramedic Coach' or 'Plumber Hunting') and no other result carries those words. Answer false if several results share its words, or the term reads like a topic, exam or job ('exam prep', 'test', 'calculator', 'scheduler', 'review' for a whole subject).

Answer true only if `search_term` reads like the title of one particular app or the name of one publisher AND a top result's title is essentially `search_term` itself (e.g. 'paramedic connect', 'carpentry formulator', 'trucker eta planner'), even when its words are ordinary. Answer false when it is a profession or topic plus a generic word like review, prep, test, guide, log, calculator or tool that many unrelated apps share ('paramedic airway review', 'chiropractic exam prep', 'pilot logbook').

Decide in two steps. 1) Does the first result's title or developer repeat ALL the distinctive words of `search_term` (not just a topic word like 'paramedic' or 'pilot')? If yes it is a name: answer true, even when the words are ordinary ('Paramedic Coach', 'Pharmacy Technician Letter'). 2) If `search_term` is a topic/task/exam phrase ('airway review', 'exam prep 2026', 'flashcards', 'calculator') and several results share those words in different titles, answer false. Do not answer true just because one result is similar; do not answer false just because the words are common.

Decide whether `search_term` is the exact title of one specific app, company or person. Compare it with the first result in `top_results`: if the term matches that app's title (or its title minus a tagline, punctuation or a generic suffix like 'Pro', 'Lite', 'Daily') and the other results are unrelated to it, answer true. If the term is a phrase anyone would type to find a kind of app, such as a topic, exam, job or task, answer false even if one app reuses those words in its name.

Is `search_term` written like a title: a short Title-Case-style label for one product, publication, course or person (e.g. 'Paramedic Coach', 'Pharmacy Technician Letter', 'Pilot Driver App') rather than a request sentence? Ordinary words can still be a name when they read as a label for one thing; a phrase like 'free X for Y' or 'best X app' is a description, not a name. Check `top_results` for one result with the same distinctive title.

Imagine `search_term` printed on an app icon or store title. If it reads like a finished product title (a distinctive word plus a generic one, e.g. 'Hvac Buddy', 'Nccaom Acupuncture Mastery') it is a name; if it is only a bare job, topic or tool a person would type to find any app ('firefighter radio', 'dental assistant temp'), it is not. Use `top_results` to confirm: the same title appearing first means a name.

Decide whether `search_term` is the name of one specific app, publisher or organization. Compare it with the titles in `top_results`: it is a name only if its distinctive words (not generic words like exam, prep, tester, tracker, calculator, guide, review) are repeated together as the title or developer of a result. A term made only of a profession, an exam or acronym, and generic task words (e.g. 'danb exam prep', 'internet speed meter & tester') is not a name even when results contain similar titles.

Is `search_term` the title of one specific app or the name of one publisher, even when it is built from ordinary words plus a role or product word (e.g. 'paramedic coach', 'pilot driver app', 'pharmacy technician letter')? Answer no when it only names a trade, exam, tool or genre (e.g. 'bartender game', 'sailing instruments', 'compass maps') that many unrelated apps would use as their title words. Check `top_results`: one result carrying the exact words as its title or publisher suggests a name; many different publishers sharing the words suggest a description.

Is `search_term` the name of ONE app or publisher? Look for a top result whose title or developer carries every distinctive word of `search_term` (ignore case, punctuation, taglines, numbers, and words like app, pro, guide, tool, kit, companion, mastery, master). Answer true if exactly one publisher owns such a title, even when the words sound descriptive (e.g. 'welding eng. guide', 'vet tech companion', 'trucker kit'). Answer false if the words are only a subject, exam, profession or tool type that several unrelated publishers reuse in their titles.

Does `search_term` name ONE specific product, app, publisher or person? Ordinary words plus a role noun ('paramedic coach', 'pilot driver app', 'pharmacy technician letter') can still be one app's title: if a top result's title or developer contains these words in this order, answer true. If the words only describe a topic and every result repeats them generically ('paramedic airway review'), answer false.

Does `search_term` look like the title of one specific app or the name of one publisher? Treat it as a name (true) when it is a short title-like phrase (often 2-4 words, possibly with a colon, 'Pro', 'Coach', 'Prep', 'Letter' or 'driver' attached) that matches or nearly matches the title of the first results in `top_results`, even though each word is ordinary. Treat it as a description (false) when it is a plain phrase a person would type to find any app for a task, such as '<topic> review', '<topic> calculator' or '<topic> practice questions', and several results with different titles and publishers all match it equally.

Decide whether `search_term` is the name of ONE specific app, company, clinic, publisher or person. A fully generic phrase for a task, exam, tool or topic (e.g. 'pharmacy technician exam prep', 'paramedic airway review') is false even when one result uses exactly those words as its title; a short phrase that is clearly a title with an added word such as coach, driver, letter, test or app (e.g. 'paramedic coach', 'pilot driver app') is true when `top_results` shows one result whose title or developer repeats its distinctive words, and false when many unrelated results share the words.

Look at the tail of `search_term`: a trailing role or format word such as coach, driver, letter, review, prep, test or app may be part of a title (e.g. 'paramedic coach', 'pharmacy technician letter', 'pilot driver app'). Answer true if a result's title or developer starts with the distinctive words of `search_term` and extra words are only such a tail; answer false if the words describe a topic, exam or tool that many results share (e.g. 'paramedic airway review', 'personal trainer prep: test' where several unrelated titles repeat the phrase).

instructions: Does `top_results[{i}]` directly serve what a person searching `search_term` wants?
Is `top_results[{i}]` built mainly for the need expressed by `search_term`, so that a searcher would pick it to solve exactly that need?

Judge `top_results[{i}]` by its own name and description, not by its category or how popular it is. Would someone who typed `search_term` install it and find that exact need solved, even if the app is niche or small?

Imagine the searcher of `search_term` has one concrete job in mind. Does `top_results[{i}]` exist to do that same job for that same kind of user (not merely the same industry, a broader weather/security/utility category, or a neighbouring job)?

Read `top_results[{i}]`'s description for what it is mainly for. Would a person who typed `search_term` install it for exactly that task? Answer yes for a dedicated tool, chart or reference for it, even if small; answer no for a broad app (weather, security, general utility) that only includes it as one feature, or for a neighbouring task with a similar name.

Compare what `top_results[{i}]` is actually for with what the searcher of `search_term` wants to do. Answer yes only if the app's own title or description says it does that exact job for that user: a dedicated calculator, chart, tracker or reference for it counts, even if small. Answer no if the app is a client-side or customer-side tool for a different audience, a general utility/weather/security app, a store or service of the same trade, or its name merely shares words with the search.

Would a person who typed `search_term` stop searching after installing `top_results[{i}]`? Check the app's own name and description: yes only if its main purpose is that exact task for the same kind of user (a dedicated calculator, chart or tracker counts, even if small); no if it is a broader suite, a customer-facing client app of a service, a neighbouring task, or merely shares words with the search.

First name the single job and the user behind `search_term`. Then read only the title and first lines of `top_results[{i}]`: answer yes if that app was clearly made for that same job and user, even if it is tiny or its name is generic. Answer no if it targets the customers of the trade instead of its professionals, is a broad weather, security or general-purpose app that only offers this as one feature, or covers a neighbouring job that merely shares words with the search.

Take the one job behind `search_term`.
